procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 05.06.2017 of the High Court of Karnataka at Dharwad Bench in MFA No.20469/2012(MV).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A learned Single Judge of the Karnataka High Court heard an appeal (MFA No.20469/2012(MV)) against an award of the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT), Belgaum. The High Court absolved the insurer.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Divisional Manager, United India Insurance Co. Ltd. and Ors. appealed the High Court's judgment to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the order of the Tribunal.

directions: The impugned judgment of the High Court absolving the insurer is set aside.
The order of the Tribunal is restored.
There shall be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether an insurer can raise the defence of negligence on the part of the victim to counter a claim for compensation in a proceeding under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.

facts: The parents of a deceased car driver filed a claim for compensation under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
The driver died after his car dashed into a truck.
The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal awarded compensation, noting that under Section 163A, proof of negligence is not required.
The insurer appealed to the High Court, which overturned the Tribunal's award.
The High Court reasoned that Section 163A is meant for innocent third parties, not for the driver who was the 'tortfeasor' (the person at fault) and responsible for the accident.
The parents of the deceased driver then appealed this decision to the Supreme Court.
law: The Supreme Court relied on its previous three-judge bench decision in *United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Sunil Kumar & Anr.*
This precedent established that the legislative intent behind Section 163A is to provide 'final compensation within a limited time frame on the basis of the structured formula'.
The purpose of this section is to overcome the long delays associated with claims based on proving fault, which are handled under Section 166 of the Act.
Allowing an insurer to raise a defense of negligence would make a Section 163A proceeding equivalent to a Section 166 proceeding, which would be self-contradictory and defeat the legislative intent.
application: The Supreme Court stated that the issue was 'no longer res integra' (already settled) due to the *Sunil Kumar* judgment.
It held that permitting the insurer to argue that the deceased driver was negligent is inconsistent with the object of Section 163A.
The Court reasoned that if such a defense were allowed, it would bring the proceeding under Section 163A on par with a proceeding under Section 166, which requires proving fault.
This would defeat the entire purpose of Section 163A, which was specifically created to provide a swift, no-fault-based remedy.
Therefore, the High Court was wrong to absolve the insurer by considering the deceased driver's alleged negligence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that in a proceeding under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act, an insurer cannot raise the defence of negligence on the part of the victim. Consequently, the Court set aside the High Court's judgment and restored the Tribunal's original award of compensation to the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an insurer can raise the defence of negligence on the part of the victim to counter a claim for compensation in a proceeding under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
appellant_arguments: A claim petition under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, does not require proving that the accident was caused by the rash and negligent act of the driver.

Allowing an insurer to raise the defense of negligence would be inconsistent with the legislative intent behind Section 163A, which is to provide final compensation within a limited time frame based on a structured formula.
Permitting a negligence defense would equate a proceeding under Section 163A with one under Section 166, defeating the purpose of the no-fault liability provision.
respondent_arguments: Section 163A is intended to compensate innocent third-party victims, not the driver who was the tortfeasor and responsible for causing the accident.
Since the deceased driver was responsible for the accident, his legal heirs are not entitled to compensation under this provision.

cases.case_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Sunil Kumar & Anr.
cases.principle: In a proceeding under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the insurer cannot raise any defence of negligence on the part of the victim to counter a claim for compensation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In a proceeding under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, an insurer cannot raise any defence of negligence on the part of the victim to counter a claim for compensation.
obiter: Allowing an insurer to raise a defence of negligence under Section 163A of the Act would be inconsistent with the legislative object of providing final compensation within a limited time frame on the basis of a structured formula.

Permitting a defence of negligence would bring a proceeding under Section 163A of the Act at par with a proceeding under Section 166 of the Act, which would be self-contradictory and defeat the legislative intention.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In a proceeding under Section 163A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, an insurer cannot raise any defence of negligence on the part of the victim to counter a claim for compensation. The court's reasoning is based entirely on the precedent set in *United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Sunil Kumar & Anr.*, which held that allowing such a defense would be inconsistent with the legislative object of the provision.
legal_tests_applied: The court applies a test of statutory interpretation that evaluates whether permitting a particular defense (negligence) is consistent with the legislative object behind the introduction of the statutory provision (Section 163A).
policy_considerations: The legislative object behind Section 163A is to provide "final compensation within a limited time frame on the basis of the structured formula to overcome situations where the claims of compensation on the basis of fault liability was taking an unduly long time".

Allowing an insurer to raise a defense of negligence would "bring a proceeding under Section 163A of the Act at par with the proceeding under Section 166 of the Act which would not only be self-contradictory but also defeat the very legislative intention".
